messages.content:
The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighLatency on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T03:22:54Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T03:23:16Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came 6 minutes 54 seconds {detection_gap} after its series passed its line, within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
Broken from 2026-11-11T03:15:00Z {began} (the onset) to 2026-11-11T03:23:43Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 8 minutes 43 seconds {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 2 minutes 57 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T03:26:12Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 0.9% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 1.4% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 2.0% {errors_at_worst} - no higher than the worst minutes of stretches as long before it began.
Rise above baseline: none beyond its normal variation - stretches as long before it began averaged as high on their own.
The series behind the alert, `max(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"}) * 1000` - its alert said "p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 215.23333333333332 ms {series_before} before it began, 1033.75 ms {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 1811 ms {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
No rise in failed requests was measured, so the harm to report is what this series did: say what it meant for the people using the service, not that little or nothing failed.
Customer loss: none - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-11-11T03:23:15Z {T1.1} Argus: Received HighLatency on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-11-11T03:23:19Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-11-11T03:23:19Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-11-11T03:23:27Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 03:22:54 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-11-11T03:23:32Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 361 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-11-11T03:23:33Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 03:15 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-11-11T03:23:33Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - [T8] 2026-11-11T03:23:35Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 {T8.2} day 1 {T8.3} minute before Nov 11 03:16 {T8.4}
  - [T9] 2026-11-11T03:23:36Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 0 {T9.2} production changes
  - [T10] 2026-11-11T03:23:37Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 2 {T10.2} candidate causes, best first: C1, C2
  - [T11] 2026-11-11T03:23:37Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Did not read logs
  - [T12] 2026-11-11T03:23:37Z {T12.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 {T12.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T12.3} hour before 03:23:37 {T12.4}
  - [T13] 2026-11-11T03:23:41Z {T13.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
  - [T14] 2026-11-11T03:23:41Z {T14.1} Argus: Called in the Mitigation Agent
  - [T15] 2026-11-11T03:23:43Z {T15.1} Mitigation Agent: Raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop for C1
  - [T16] 2026-11-11T03:23:50Z {T16.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 03:24 {T16.2} - up to 196s {T16.3}
  - [T17] 2026-11-11T03:26:12Z {T17.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 03:23 {T17.2}
  - [T18] 2026-11-11T03:26:12Z {T18.1} Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  - [T19] 2026-11-11T03:26:12Z {T19.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - raised [io-shop]'s autoscaler floor from [3 {T19.2}] replicas to [6 {T19.3}] and the rule that fired stopped firing
  - [T20] 2026-11-11T03:28:13Z {T20.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/544

Changes to production it read:
  - Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - Not read.

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1, also C2] Candidates blaming the same move of io-shop, each reading it as a different kind of failure - different accounts of what it did, not one cause counted twice - each in its own words:
      C1: Capacity will not settle: cpu_limit_cores flips between 3.0 {C1.1} and 6.0 {C1.2} from 2026-11-11T03:11:00Z {C1.3} onward while traffic climbs. In the minutes served at 3.0 {C1.4} cores, CPU is pinned at the limit and p95 jumps to 1.3-1.8s {C1.5}. In the minutes served at 6.0 {C1.6} cores, p95 returns to about 212ms {C1.7}. Nothing was deployed. [autoscaling-pathology, confidence 0.6 {C1.8}, confirmed]
      C2: Request volume rose from 1200 {C1.9} to 5400 {C1.10} req/min starting 2026-11-11T03:10:00Z {C1.11}. This outgrew the 3-core allocation, so CPU saturated and requests queued, pushing p95 up. [demand-saturation, confidence 0.3 {C1.12}, confirmed, as tested for C1]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop for [C1] (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] deploy/values-production.yaml renders the shop's HorizontalPodAutoscaler with minReplicas 3 {F1.1}, maxReplicas 6 {F1.2}, targetCpuPercent 70 {F1.3} and scaleDownStabilizationSeconds 0 {F1.4}. The file's own comment says what that window is for: Kubernetes defaults it to 300 {F1.5} seconds, so the controller acts on the highest recommendation from the last five minutes. Otherwise it acts on a reading that its own last action produced.
      
      At 0 {F1.6} the loop flaps. At 3 {F1.7} replicas CPU is pinned, so the controller scales to 6 {F1.8}. At 6 {F1.9} replicas the per-replica CPU falls below target, and with no window the controller scales straight back to 3 {F1.10} on that reading, which pins CPU again. That fits the capacity the investigation saw moving between 3.0 {F1.11} and 6.0 {F1.12} cores. The 6-to-3 flip is one minute after a scale-up, while traffic is still climbing.
      
      This change sets scaleDownStabilizationSeconds to 300 {F1.13}, the Kubernetes default. Scale-up is unchanged and happens as soon as it is needed. Scale-down now only happens once the higher recommendation has held for five minutes, so the post-scale-up dip can no longer undo the scale-up.
      
      Nothing under src/ reads the autoscaling block (a search for scaleDownStabilization matches only this file), so no service code or tests need to change. There is no test because the fix is in deployment configuration, not code this repository's tests exercise.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
  - AI-3 (mitigate, open): Turn automatic sync of io-shop back on once its repository says what should run - until then nothing merged reaches it, and turned on sooner it puts back what the repository says, undoing what Argus changed by hand
PR #544 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: The production values for io-shop's HorizontalPodAutoscaler set its scale-down stabilization window to {F1.4} seconds. As Code-Fix reads it, after scaling up from {F1.1} to {F1.2} replicas, the controller acted straight away on the lower per-replica CPU that its own scale-up had produced. It scaled back to {F1.1} replicas, where CPU was pinned again, so serving capacity kept flipping up and down instead of holding. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
cause_in_plain_words: The shop's automatic scaling likely kept taking away the extra servers it had just added, because a setting meant to make it wait before scaling back down was set to zero, and that left too few servers to answer requests quickly.
still_at_risk: While the scale-down window in the shop's configuration stays at zero, the autoscaler could again drop the shop back to too few replicas as soon as its floor is lowered, and responses could slow again.
symptom: Shop requests responded far more slowly than usual
causal_chain 1: People using the shop got much slower responses: its slowest requests took far longer than usual, while failed requests stayed within their normal variation. (cites AL1; T6, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 2: Responses slowed because io-shop had too little serving capacity for the requests coming in. (cites T17, under "What Argus did, in order"; T18, under "What Argus did, in order"; T19, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 3: It had too little capacity because the autoscaler did not hold the higher replica count. It kept taking the service back down to its floor of {T7.2} replicas, the count read at {T7.1}. (cites T7, under "What Argus did, in order"; T19, under "What Argus did, in order"; F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix")
causal_chain 4: The autoscaler scaled back down straight away because the production values set its scale-down stabilization window to {F1.4} seconds. That let it act on the low per-replica CPU that its own scale-up had produced. (cites F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix")
contributing_factors 1: No check was seen that would have stopped a production autoscaler configuration with a scale-down stabilization window of zero from going out.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: The window would have stayed at a non-zero value such as the default. The autoscaler would then have held its scale-up, and capacity would not have kept dropping back to the floor.
contributing_factors 2: No alert was seen on the autoscaler repeatedly scaling io-shop up and back down. The fault was found only by the latency alert.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: The flapping could have been caught from the replica count itself, before slow responses had gone on long enough to set off the latency alert.
action_items 1: Add a CI check that rejects production autoscaler values with a scale-down stabilization window of zero, or below an agreed minimum, for every service.
action_items 2: Add an alert that fires when a service's autoscaler keeps reversing its replica count within a short window.
action_items 3: Link io-shop's HighLatency alert to the on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.
went_wrong 1: The alert fired on the production shop, but no on-call incident was linked to it, so nobody was paged.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.

tools.name: judge_claims
